strings.registries/VERBS/0/tip: The most important verb. Use it for identity, origin, state and place.
strings.registries/VERBS/1/tip: Also used for age (ho 28 anni) and feelings (ho fame, ho sete). The h is silent.
strings.registries/VERBS/2/tip: Use a with cities (vado a Roma) and in with countries (vado in Italia).
strings.registries/VERBS/4/tip: To be polite use "vorrei" (I would like): Vorrei un caffè, per favore.
strings.registries/VERBS/5/tip: Followed by another verb in the infinitive: posso parlare, puoi venire.
strings.registries/VERBS/6/tip: Opposite of andare. Takes essere in the past: sono venuto/a.
strings.registries/VERBS/8/tip: Model regular -are verb. Most Italian verbs follow this pattern.
strings.registries/VERBS/9/tip: Verbs in -giare drop the i before another i (tu mangi, not mangii).
strings.registries/VERBS/10/tip: Regular -ere verb in the present. The past participle is irregular (visto).
strings.registries/VERBS/11/tip: Model regular -ire verb. Note the noi and voi forms keep the stress on the ending.

strings.modules/TOPICS#1/0/s: Italian is spelled the way it sounds
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/0/sec/0/p: Every letter is pronounced. The vowels are short and clear: a (ah), e (eh), i (ee), o (oh), u (oo). Never glide them like in English.
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/0/sec/1/h: C and G change before e and i
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/0/sec/1/p: Before e or i, c sounds like "ch" and g like "j". Before a, o, u they are hard: k and g. Add an h to keep them hard before e or i.
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/0/sec/2/p: gn is like "ny" in canyon. gli is like "lli" in million. sc before e or i is "sh". sch is "sk".
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/0/sec/3/p: Double letters are held longer. It can change the meaning, so listen closely.
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/0/sec/4/p: Most words are stressed on the second to last syllable (a-MI-co). A written accent shows stress on the last syllable.
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/0/q/0/0: How do you say the start of "cena"?
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/0/q/0/3: Before e or i, c is "ch".
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/0/q/1/0: "che" (what) is pronounced with which first sound?
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/0/q/1/3: ch + h keeps the hard k sound.
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/1/sec/0/p: The article depends on gender, number and the first letter of the next word.
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/1/sec/1/p: Un (masc.), uno (before s+consonant or z), una (fem.), un' (fem. before a vowel). Careful: un amico has no apostrophe, but un'amica does.
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/2/sec/0/p: Most nouns ending in -o are masculine, in -a feminine. Nouns in -e can be either, so learn them with their article.
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/2/sec/2/p: -ca and -ga become -che and -ghe to keep the hard sound. -co usually becomes -chi or -ci. Some words never change: nouns ending in an accent, and foreign words.
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/3/sec/0/p: Italian verbs end in -are, -ere or -ire. Remove the ending to get the stem, then add the endings for each person.
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/3/sec/1/p: The ending already tells who is acting, so Italians usually drop io, tu, noi... Use them only for emphasis.
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/3/sec/1/ex/1/1: I speak Italian, he speaks French.
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/4/s: To be and to have, and when to use each
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/4/sec/0/p: Use essere for identity, nationality, origin, profession, state, and location.
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/4/sec/1/p: Use avere for possession, and for age and many feelings, where English uses "to be".
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/5/sec/0/p: For yes or no questions, keep the word order and raise your intonation at the end.
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/5/sec/1/p: Learn these eight and you can ask almost anything.
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/5/q/0/3: Come = how, literally "how do you call yourself".
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/6/sec/0/p: To make a sentence negative, place non right before the verb.
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/6/sec/1/p: Italian keeps non and adds another negative word after the verb: niente, mai, nessuno.
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/6/sec/2/p: Subject, verb, object, like English. Adjectives usually come after the noun.
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/7/sec/0/p: a = to/at (cities), di = of/from, da = from/at someone's, in = in/to (countries), su = on, con = with, per = for, tra/fra = between/in.
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/7/sec/0/ex/4/1: I go out with a friend.
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/7/sec/1/p: a, di, da, in and su merge with the article.
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/7/sec/1/ex/0/1: The book is on the table.
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/8/sec/0/p: Adjectives change with the noun: -o, -a, -i, -e. Adjectives in -e only change for number (grande, grandi). They usually come after the noun.
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/8/sec/1/p: Italian uses the article with possessives: il mio libro. With singular family members the article is dropped: mia madre.
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/8/q/0/3: Casa is feminine singular, so nera.
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/8/q/2/3: Singular family members drop the article.

strings.modules/TOPICS#1/9/sec/0/p: 11-16 end in -dici. 17-19 are "ten and seven" (diciassette). After that, tens drop the last vowel before uno and otto: ventuno, ventotto.
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/9/sec/1/p: Days and months are not capitalised in Italian.
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/9/sec/3/p: Use essere in the plural for hours (sono le tre), but singular for one o'clock, noon and midnight.

strings.modules/CULT#1/0/2: Italians drink cappuccino at breakfast, not after meals. After lunch or dinner, ask for un caffè, which means an espresso.
strings.modules/CULT#1/1/2: Many restaurants add a small cover charge per person, called il coperto. It is normal and is shown on the menu or bill.
strings.modules/CULT#1/2/2: Use Lei (formal) with strangers, older people and in shops. Use tu with friends, family and children.
strings.modules/CULT#1/3/2: Pranzo (lunch) is around 12:30 to 14:00. Cena (dinner) usually starts after 20:00, so restaurants can be empty earlier.
strings.modules/CULT#1/4/2: A coffee standing at the bar counter (al banco) costs less than the same coffee at a table.
strings.modules/CULT#1/5/2: For many regional train paper tickets you must stamp them in the machine on the platform before boarding (convalidare).
strings.modules/CULT#1/6/2: Use buongiorno and buonasera in shops, hotels and with people you do not know. Ciao is for friends and people your age.
strings.modules/CULT#1/7/2: A full meal goes: antipasto, primo (pasta or rice), secondo (meat or fish), contorno (side), dolce, caffè. You can skip courses.
strings.modules/CULT#1/8/2: In smaller towns many shops close in the early afternoon and reopen around 16:00 or 17:00.
strings.modules/CULT#1/9/2: Friends often greet with two kisses on the cheeks. With new people in a work setting, a handshake is safer.
strings.modules/VERBS.push#1/0/tip: Like volere and potere, it is followed by an infinitive: devo andare.
strings.modules/VERBS.push#1/1/ex/1: I know how to speak Italian.
strings.modules/VERBS.push#1/1/tip: Use sapere for facts and skills. Use conoscere for people and places.
strings.modules/VERBS.push#1/2/tip: The past participle is irregular: detto. Also used in "come si dice...?" (how do you say...?).
strings.modules/VERBS.push#1/3/ex/1: How are you? I am well.
strings.modules/VERBS.push#1/3/tip: Used for health and feelings (sto bene) and for "sto + gerund" (sto mangiando, I am eating).
strings.modules/VERBS.push#1/4/tip: The stem changes: esc- when stressed, usc- in noi and voi.
strings.modules/VERBS.push#1/5/tip: Very common when ordering: prendo la pasta. The participle is irregular: preso.
strings.modules/VERBS.push#1/6/tip: An -isc- verb: io, tu, lui and loro add -isc- before the ending. Many -ire verbs work this way (finire, preferire).
strings.modules/VERBS.push#1/7/tip: Regular in the present. The participle is irregular: letto. Double g keeps the hard sound: leggo.
strings.modules/TOPICS.push#1/0/sec/0/p: Use avere or essere in the present, then the past participle. For -are verbs the participle ends in -ato, for -ere in -uto, for -ire in -ito.
strings.modules/TOPICS.push#1/0/sec/1/p: Verbs of movement and change use essere, and the participle agrees with the subject: andare, venire, arrivare, partire, uscire, essere, nascere. A woman says sono andata, a man sono andato.
strings.modules/TOPICS.push#1/0/sec/2/p: Learn these by heart. They appear all the time.
strings.modules/TOPICS.push#1/0/q/1/3: Andare takes essere, and andata agrees with Maria.

strings.modules/TOPICS.push#1/1/sec/1/p: Many daily actions are reflexive in Italian. Note that "mi chiamo" literally means "I call myself".
strings.modules/TOPICS.push#1/1/sec/1/ex/2/1: I get dressed and go out.
strings.modules/TOPICS.push#1/1/sec/2/p: Reflexive verbs always take essere in the passato prossimo.
strings.modules/TOPICS.push#1/1/sec/2/ex/1/1: She had a lot of fun.
strings.modules/TOPICS.push#1/2/sec/0/p: Italian does not say "I like". It says the thing pleases me. So the verb matches the thing you like: piace for one thing or an action, piacciono for several things.
strings.modules/TOPICS.push#1/2/sec/1/p: Change the small word: mi (me), ti (you), gli (him), le (her), ci (us), vi (you all), gli (them).
strings.modules/TOPICS.push#1/2/q/2/0: How do you say "I do not like coffee"?
strings.modules/TOPICS.push#1/3/sec/0/p: Volere (want), potere (can) and dovere (must) are followed by a verb in the infinitive. Only the first verb changes.
strings.modules/TOPICS.push#1/3/sec/1/p: Use vorrei (I would like) to order or ask. It sounds softer than voglio.

strings.modules/TOPICS.push#1/3/sec/2/p: Use sapere + infinitive for a learned skill.

strings.modules/TOPICS.push#2/0/sec/0/p: Take the infinitive, drop the final -e and change -are to -er. Then add the endings: -ò, -ai, -à, -emo, -ete, -anno. For -ere and -ire verbs the stem is simply -er and -ir.
strings.modules/TOPICS.push#2/0/sec/1/p: Verbs in -care and -gare add an h to keep the hard sound: cercherò, pagherò. Verbs in -ciare and -giare lose the i: mangerò, comincerò.
strings.modules/TOPICS.push#2/0/sec/2/p: Many common verbs change the stem but keep the same endings.
strings.modules/TOPICS.push#2/0/sec/3/p: Italians often use the present for the near future (domani vado a Roma). The future also expresses a guess about now: Sarà a casa means He is probably at home.
strings.modules/TOPICS.push#2/0/sec/3/ex/0/1: Tomorrow I am going to Rome.
strings.modules/TOPICS.push#2/0/sec/3/ex/1/1: I wonder what time it is.
strings.modules/TOPICS.push#2/0/q/1/3: Andare has the stem andr-: andremo.
strings.modules/TOPICS.push#2/0/q/2/3: Essere has the stem sar-: sarò.
strings.modules/TOPICS.push#2/1/sec/0/p: When a, di, da, in or su meets the article (il, la, lo...), they join into one word. This happens all the time, so it is worth learning once.
strings.modules/TOPICS.push#2/1/sec/1/ex/5/1: The keys are on the chair.
strings.modules/TOPICS.push#2/1/sec/2/p: The preposition in stays separate before a name or with no article: in Italia, in casa, a Roma, a scuola.
strings.modules/TOPICS.push#2/2/sec/0/p: For -are verbs the command is the same as lui: parla! For -ere and -ire verbs it is the same as tu: scrivi! dormi! To say do not, use non + infinitive.
strings.modules/TOPICS.push#2/2/sec/1/p: To a stranger, an older person or in a shop, use the Lei form. -are verbs end in -i. -ere and -ire verbs end in -a.
strings.modules/TOPICS.push#2/2/sec/2/p: A few very common commands are irregular.
